posts.title: Flexibility Without Coherence: What Sustainability Reports Reveal About IFRS S1
posts.body:
> Can I tell whether a company has meaningfully applied IFRS S1?

I recently reviewed a range of published sustainability reports with that one question in mind. Across industries — including professional services — I noticed two recurring patterns.

The first was reports that disclosed little more than SASB metrics. While SASB standards are an important reference within IFRS S1, they are not the framework itself. IFRS S1 requires connected disclosures across governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. Reporting metrics without explaining how sustainability risks are identified, managed, and linked to financial performance provides only part of the picture.

The second pattern was more subtle. Some reports appeared comprehensive, but the information was spread across annual reports, sustainability reports, management commentary, and other referenced documents. Although the disclosures were technically available, understanding the complete story required navigating multiple documents and piecing together information prepared in different contexts.

Importantly, most of the companies I reviewed did not claim compliance with IFRS S1. This is therefore not a question of non-compliance. Rather, it highlights a broader issue: partial or informal alignment with IFRS S1 without demonstrating a coherent application of its principles.

This points to an implementation challenge within the standard. IFRS S1 intentionally provides flexibility through materiality judgments and cross-referencing. That flexibility is valuable. However, without sufficient guardrails, it can also result in fragmented reporting that makes it difficult for investors and other users to understand the complete picture.

As IFRS S1 becomes mandatory in more jurisdictions, this issue will become increasingly important. Reporting practices established during the voluntary phase are likely to influence how mandatory reporting evolves.

Several practical enhancements could improve usability without reducing flexibility:

- A disclosure index mapping IFRS S1 requirements to their location.
- Limits on layered cross-referencing for material disclosures.
- Greater transparency around materiality assessments.
- Consistent assurance over material information, regardless of where it is published.

IFRS S1 was developed to improve the consistency, comparability, and decision-usefulness of sustainability reporting. My review of published reports suggests that achieving those objectives will require more than flexibility alone. It will also require greater coherence.

Flexibility without coherence is not merely an implementation issue — it is one of the key challenges that the next phase of IFRS S1 adoption should address.
